questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis with indurated edges and a clean base, developing 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse. Regional lymph nodes are firm and non-tender. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: The classic Hunterian chancre of primary syphilis is a painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base caused by Treponema pallidum. Haemophilus ducreyi causes soft, painful chancroid ulcers. HSV ulcers are painful and vesicular. Klebsiella granulomatis causes donovanosis with beefy-red granulation tissue.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops tense bullae on sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed skin. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blistering with neutrophilic infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA, IgG, and IgM at the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous SLE is characterised by subepidermal bullae in a patient with SLE, neutrophilic infiltrate, and immunoreactants (IgG, IgM, IgA) at the BMZ in a linear or granular pattern. It mimics EBA but the clinical context of SLE and the 'full house' immunofluorescence pattern distinguish it. Antibodies are directed against type VII collagen.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with verrucous plaques on the foot extending up the leg after a thorn prick injury 2 years ago. KOH mount shows brown, thick-walled, septate sclerotic bodies in a copper-penny arrangement. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous plaques after traumatic inoculation and is characterised by 'copper-penny' or 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies) on histology. Fonsecaea pedrosoi is the most common cause in India. Sporothrix causes lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. Madurella causes eumycetoma. Rhinocladiella causes cerebral phaeohyphomycosis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple anaesthetic hypopigmented patches and nodular lesions. Slit-skin smear from the ear lobe is strongly positive (BI 5+). Nerve biopsy shows foamy macrophages laden with AFB and a Grenz zone in the upper dermis. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) has the highest bacterial load (BI 4-6+). Histologically, foamy (Virchow) macrophages stuffed with AFB in globi, a Grenz zone (clear subepidermal zone), and absent cell-mediated immunity (no granuloma) are characteristic. It represents the anergic pole of the leprosy spectrum with widespread lesions and nerve involvement.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a firm, flesh-coloured nodule on the lower lip that has been growing for 3 months. Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, stromal retraction artefact, and mucin deposition. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is characterised by nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction (peritumoral clefting) on histology. Although BCC rarely occurs on the lip, these histological features are diagnostic. SCC shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Merkel cell carcinoma shows CK20 positivity. Keratoacanthoma shows a crater filled with keratin.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. She also has a positive pathergy test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet disease is characterised by the triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Pathergy (papule or pustule formation 24-48 hours after a needle prick) is a hallmark finding. HLA-B51 is strongly associated. Reiter syndrome has urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis. Sweet syndrome is a neutrophilic dermatosis with fever and tender plaques.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with targetoid skin lesions on the palms and dorsa of hands following a herpes labialis outbreak. The lesions have a central dusky area, a surrounding pale ring, and an outer erythematous ring. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme (EM) minor is characterised by classic three-zone target lesions typically triggered by HSV, predominantly affecting acral areas. EM minor has <10% BSA involvement and no or minimal mucosal involvement. SJS has mucosal involvement at ≥2 sites and epidermal detachment. Fixed drug eruption leaves post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on long-term penicillamine for rheumatoid arthritis develops skin fragility, milia, and haemorrhagic bullae on sun-exposed areas with normal porphyrin levels. What is the mechanism of this drug reaction?
opts: Photosensitisation leading to subepidermal blister formation
questions.exp: Penicillamine can cause pseudoporphyria — a porphyria cutanea tarda-like picture with photosensitivity, skin fragility, milia, and scarring on sun-exposed sites, but with normal porphyrin levels. The mechanism involves UV-induced subepidermal blistering. NSAIDs (especially naproxen) are another common cause. Drug-induced pemphigus (also seen with penicillamine) is a separate entity showing acantholysis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of the exudate shows Gram-positive cocci in chains. The most appropriate first-line topical antibiotic is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (and/or Staphylococcus aureus) presents with honey-coloured crusts. Topical mupirocin (2%) is the first-line topical treatment and is highly effective against both organisms. Fusidic acid is an alternative. Topical clindamycin is used mainly for acne. Neomycin has poor streptococcal coverage and high sensitisation rates.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with a 20-year history of psoriasis develops tender erythematous plaques with fever and neutrophilia. Biopsy shows spongiform pustules of Kogoj in the upper epidermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Generalised pustular psoriasis (GPP, von Zumbusch type) presents with acute onset of sterile pustules on an erythematous base with fever and systemic toxicity, often triggered by withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. Histology shows spongiform pustules of Kogoj (neutrophil-filled intraepidermal pustules). AGEP is drug-induced. Munro microabscesses (in the corneal layer) are seen in chronic plaque psoriasis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with pruritic papules and plaques on the flexures of elbows and knees with lichenification. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Which cytokine is primarily responsible for the IgE class switching in this condition?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis is a Th2-mediated disease. IL-4 and IL-13 are the key cytokines responsible for IgE class switching in B cells and are central to the pathogenesis. They also downregulate filaggrin expression, contributing to barrier dysfunction. Dupilumab targets the shared IL-4Rα receptor of both. IL-12 and IFN-gamma are Th1 cytokines. IL-17 is key in psoriasis pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female presents with symmetric hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead that worsens in summer. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of the pigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Melasma (chloasma) presents with symmetric macular hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed facial areas, predominantly in women, worsening with UV exposure. It is associated with pregnancy, OCPs, and thyroid disorders. Wood's lamp accentuates epidermal (but not dermal) melasma. Treatment includes photoprotection, hydroquinone, triple combination cream (hydroquinone + retinoid + steroid), and chemical peels.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer with long-term arsenic exposure presents with multiple hyperkeratotic papules on the palms and soles, Mees' lines on nails, and rain-drop pigmentation on the trunk. Which malignancy is he at highest risk of developing in the skin?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma and Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
questions.exp: Chronic arsenic exposure leads to arsenical keratoses (palmoplantar), rain-drop pigmentation, and Mees' lines. Arsenic is a recognised carcinogen for SCC (arising in Bowen's disease/arsenical keratoses) and multiple BCCs, especially on non-sun-exposed areas. It also increases risk of internal malignancies (lung, bladder, liver). Arsenic-related BCCs are superficial and multiple.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with multiple flesh-coloured flat-topped papules on the dorsa of hands and face. One lesion shows central clearing. Dermoscopy reveals dotted vessels and irregular pigment network. Which HPV types are most commonly associated with this presentation?
questions.exp: Plane (flat) warts (verruca plana) are caused by HPV types 3 and 10. They present as flat-topped, skin-coloured to slightly pigmented papules on the face, dorsa of hands, and legs. HPV 6 and 11 cause anogenital condylomata acuminata. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types associated with cervical and oropharyngeal carcinoma. HPV 1 and 2 cause common warts (verruca vulgaris).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with dysphagia and Raynaud's phenomenon presents with tightening of facial skin, telangiectasias on the face, and sclerodactyly. She has positive anti-Scl-70 antibody. This antibody targets which antigen?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and correlate with a higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome). Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with dcSSc and scleroderma renal crisis. Anti-U1-RNP is associated with mixed connective tissue disease.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging, well-defined, pearly translucent nodule with rolled edges and surface telangiectasias on the nasal ala. The surgical treatment with the highest cure rate for this lesion is:
questions.exp: This is a nodular BCC on a high-risk H-zone location (nose). Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) offers the highest cure rate (~99% for primary BCC) by providing complete peripheral and deep margin examination with tissue conservation — critical on the face. Simple excision has ~95% cure rate for primary BCC but with less margin certainty. Curettage is only appropriate for low-risk, small BCCs on the trunk/limbs.

questions.q: A neonate develops vesicles on the trunk that evolve to pustules and then to hyperpigmented macules over 48 hours. The lesions spare the palms and soles. Wright stain of pustule contents shows numerous eosinophils with no organisms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN) is a benign, self-limiting condition in term neonates. It presents with erythematous macules, papules, and pustules that characteristically spare the palms and soles. Wright stain shows eosinophils (not neutrophils). It resolves spontaneously without treatment. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis shows neutrophils on smear and affects palms/soles as well.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with non-scarring alopecia in a band-like pattern along the temporal and occipital hairline. Pull test is positive at the margins. Trichoscopy shows yellow dots and exclamation mark hairs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ophiasis is a pattern of alopecia areata affecting the occipital and temporal scalp in a band-like distribution. Trichoscopy reveals pathognomonic features: yellow dots (empty follicular infundibula filled with sebum/keratin), exclamation mark hairs (dystrophic hairs tapered proximally), and black dots (broken hairs at scalp level). It is associated with a poorer prognosis than patchy AA.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male has onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and the oil-drop sign on multiple fingernails alongside salmon-coloured plaques on elbows and scalp. Which nail finding is considered most specific for psoriatic nail disease?
questions.exp: Nail pitting (Rosenau's pits) — small, punched-out depressions on the nail surface — is the most common and most specific nail change in psoriasis, resulting from psoriatic involvement of the proximal nail matrix. The oil-drop (salmon patch) sign is highly specific for psoriasis. Onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis occur in both psoriasis and onychomycosis. Beau's lines are transverse grooves from any acute illness.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with painful nodules on the shins bilaterally, associated with fever and joint pains, 2 weeks after a throat infection treated with amoxicillin. Biopsy of the nodule shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (EN) is the most common form of panniculitis. It presents with tender red nodules on the anterior shins, triggered by streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, TB, IBD, or drugs. Histology shows septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis (Miescher's radial granulomas in septa are pathognomonic). Erythema induratum is lobular panniculitis WITH vasculitis, associated with TB. EN is self-limiting; NSAIDs and potassium iodide are used.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male forest officer presents with a painless papule on the hand that evolved into an ulcer with raised, violaceous undermined edges over one month. Biopsy shows massive fat necrosis with many AFB. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Mycobacterium ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer, characterised by painless ulcers with undermined edges due to production of mycolactone toxin causing fat necrosis and immunosuppression. The pain-free nature is due to mycolactone's analgesic effects on nerve endings. Histology shows massive necrosis with AFB. M. marinum causes swimming pool granuloma with a sporotrichoid pattern. M. leprae causes leprosy, not undermined ulcers.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male has grouped vesicles over the S2-S3 dermatome in the sacral area with 4 similar episodes in the past year. The best long-term management to prevent recurrences is:
opts: Topical acyclovir 5% cream applied at onset of each episode
Oral acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days episodically
Oral valacyclovir 500 mg once daily continuously for 1 year
Famciclovir 1500 mg as a single dose at onset
questions.exp: Recurrent genital herpes with ≥4 episodes/year warrants suppressive therapy. Valacyclovir 500 mg OD (or 1g OD) for 12 months suppresses recurrences by ~80% and reduces asymptomatic viral shedding, decreasing transmission risk. Acyclovir 400 mg BD is an alternative. Episodic therapy is appropriate for infrequent recurrences. Topical acyclovir has no role in genital herpes management.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman develops intensely pruritic violaceous, flat-topped papules on the wrists and ankles with white lacy lines on the buccal mucosa. Biopsy shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ with civatte bodies and saw-tooth rete ridges. The pathognomonic clinical finding is:
questions.exp: Wickham's striae are the pathognomonic clinical feature of lichen planus — white lacy lines visible on the surface of violaceous papules and on mucous membranes. Histologically, the band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate, saw-tooth rete ridges, hypergranulosis, and Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes) are characteristic. Max-Joseph spaces are subepidermal clefts seen histologically in lichen planus but are not pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with a 2 cm firm nodule on the right cheek that has doubled in size over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with perinuclear dot-like CK20 positivity and positive neuroendocrine markers. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Cutaneous metastasis of lung small cell carcinoma
questions.exp: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin. It shows CK20 positivity in a characteristic perinuclear dot pattern and expresses neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin). It is CK7 negative (unlike small cell lung carcinoma which is CK7+/CK20-). Rapid growth in elderly patients on sun-exposed areas is typical. Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) is found in ~80% of cases.

questions.q: A 15-year-old girl develops painful blistering on sun-exposed areas each summer, sparing covered areas. Phototesting shows abnormal UVA reaction. Which investigation confirms the specific diagnosis?
opts: Urine and stool porphyrin analysis with RBC protoporphyrin
Phototesting with UVA and UVB and provocative phototesting
questions.exp: Painful vesicular eruption exclusively in summer in a teenager with UVA sensitivity is classic for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP). In EPP, urine porphyrins may be normal; the diagnostic tests are elevated RBC protoporphyrin (free protoporphyrin) and stool porphyrins. Plasma fluorescence emission peak at 634 nm is also diagnostic. Phototesting confirms photosensitivity but porphyrin analysis identifies the specific metabolic defect.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male with HIV (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) has extensive perianal condylomata and irregular atypical plaques. What is the gold standard procedure to screen for and diagnose anal intraepithelial neoplasia?
questions.exp: High-resolution anoscopy (HRA) with targeted biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) in high-risk individuals (HIV+, MSM, immunosuppressed). Anal Pap smear is a screening tool but has low specificity; HRA allows visual inspection with acetic acid/Lugol's iodine and directed biopsy of abnormal areas. Immunosuppressed HIV-positive patients have high rates of HSIL (high-grade AIN) that can progress to anal SCC.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male leprosy patient on MDT develops acute painful erythematous nodules on the face and extensor surfaces, fever, and orchitis. Blood work shows elevated CRP and neutrophilia (ENL reaction). The first-line treatment is:
questions.exp: Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum, ENL) occurs in BL/LL leprosy and is immune complex-mediated. First-line treatment is thalidomide (400 mg/day tapering over months) due to its potent anti-TNF-α effect. Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated (women of childbearing age, due to severe teratogenicity). Clofazimine at higher doses is used for recurrent/chronic ENL. MDT should be continued throughout reactions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a verrucous, wartlike plaque on the lower leg that has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. He had pulmonary TB 5 years ago and has a strongly positive tuberculin test. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (TBVC) occurs by exogenous inoculation of M. tuberculosis into sensitised skin (positive tuberculin test), presenting as a warty, verrucous plaque typically on the hands/legs. It is seen in healthcare workers and those handling infected material. Lupus vulgaris shows soft gelatinous 'apple-jelly' nodules. Scrofuloderma is TB of skin overlying affected lymph nodes/bones. Erythema induratum is lobular panniculitis with vasculitis.

questions.q: A Tzanck smear from a fresh vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells with nuclear moulding and ground-glass chromatin. This finding is diagnostic of infection by which group of viruses?
opts: Herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster virus
questions.exp: The Tzanck smear (Tzanck test) is positive in herpesviridae infections — both HSV types 1 and 2 and VZV show multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) with nuclear moulding and ground-glass chromatin. It cannot distinguish between HSV and VZV (PCR or DFA is needed for that). Molluscum shows Henderson-Paterson bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions). Coxsackievirus blisters are Tzanck-negative. Smallpox was eradicated; vaccinia shows Guarnieri bodies.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with pruritic, tense bullae on the inner thighs and flexures arising on normal and erythematous skin, with mild eosinophilia. DIF of perilesional skin shows linear C3 and IgG at the BMZ. ELISA detects antibodies against BP180 NC16A domain. What is the most appropriate first-line systemic treatment?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterised by tense bullae, linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ (hemidesmosomal level), and anti-BP180 (type XVII collagen NC16A domain) antibodies. First-line treatment for moderate-severe BP is oral prednisolone at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day. Super-potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol propionate) are equally effective and safer in elderly patients. Dapsone is used for mild BP or as a steroid-sparing agent. Rituximab is reserved for refractory disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a yellowish plaque on the palm with thickened overlying skin and a central dimple that accentuates on lateral compression (Fitzpatrick's sign). Which enzyme deficiency is most commonly responsible for familial cases of this condition?
questions.exp: The clinical description — yellowish plaque on the palm with central dimple and Fitzpatrick's sign — describes xanthoma striata palmaris (palmar crease xanthomata), pathognomonic for type III hyperlipoproteinaemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia). This is caused by apo-E2 homozygosity (APOE ε2/ε2), which impairs clearance of IDL and chylomicron remnants. LDL receptor mutations cause familial hypercholesterolaemia with tendinous xanthomata. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes eruptive xanthomata with chylomicronaemia.
